sections.heading: Look for the shadow of a strength
sections.content: Singhal calls this the “shadows of superpowers”: a strength that helped someone succeed can create a development problem at the next level, so “what gets you there isn’t what got you here.” For example, someone may see themselves as a great collaborator because they work well with people who agree with them, but senior colleagues outside their function may recoil when that person moves quickly and pushes their view. sections.heading: Seek candid feedback—and don’t explain it away
sections.content: He recommends getting “real feedback, not formal feedback,” including ground-truth conversations with peers. Listen closely rather than immediately justifying why the feedback is wrong. Go back through prior feedback and examine what was discarded as an anomaly; don’t assume a critical comment is irrelevant because the person was upset or had some other reason to say it. As Singhal puts it, “Perception’s reality.” [S1, S3]

answer.summary: Singhal’s advice is to look for the shadow of a strength: get candid peer feedback, listen without dismissing it, and consider whether the approach that worked before needs to change at a more senior level.

sections.heading: Re-examine what “good collaboration” means
sections.content: A leader may collaborate well when others agree, yet struggle when leading with a strong point of view—especially with senior colleagues outside their function, who may recoil if the leader moves too fast. Singhal’s practical point is that a strength can create a shadow, and the tools that got someone to one level may need to be rebuilt or relearned for the next.

sections.heading: Seek ground-truth feedback and listen to the uncomfortable parts
sections.content: Singhal recommends real conversations with peers rather than relying only on formal feedback, whose signals can differ substantially. Listen without immediately explaining why the feedback is wrong. Revisit feedback that was discarded as an anomaly; managers may dismiss it as a one-off, but Singhal says to take perceptions seriously and examine whether they reveal a pattern.

sections.heading: Treat the feedback as a development signal, not proof the strength is false
sections.content: If a strength is now getting in the way, Singhal says the person may still be exercising it effectively—the challenge is that they have reached a new level. Recognizing the development area can be difficult because it is bound up with identity, but naming it is where the work of changing begins. This is advice to investigate and adapt, not a guarantee that every criticism is correct.

answer.summary: Singhal advises executives to treat a strength that now undermines collaboration as a possible “shadow of a superpower,” seek candid ground-truth feedback, and seriously examine criticism they or their managers have dismissed. A strength may have worked at an earlier level but need to be rebuilt for leadership.

sections.heading: Look for the shadow of the strength
sections.content: Singhal describes how collaboration can mean working well when others agree with your point of view; at a more senior level, moving quickly with that same approach can make people in other functions recoil. The practical implication is to ask whether a strength is being applied in a way that no longer works at the next level—not assume past praise means it cannot be a development area. He calls this a “shadow of a superpower” and says the tools that got you here may need to be rebuilt or relearned for the next phase.

sections.heading: Get candid feedback and listen without dismissing it
sections.content: Seek real conversations with peers, not just formal review systems, to get the ground truth about how people experience your behavior. Listen rather than immediately justifying why the feedback is wrong. Singhal specifically recommends revisiting prior feedback and looking at what ended up on the “discard pile”: criticism may have been labeled an anomaly or explained away by you or your managers, but he says to take it seriously—“Perception’s reality.” He says you do not need a coach to start; you do need to listen to contradictory feedback.

sections.heading: Recognize what may need to change
sections.content: The aim is not to abandon the strength, but to identify where it is getting in the way and work on that development area. Singhal notes that people can resist this because the strength is part of their identity—“This is what got me here”—and that recognizing the pattern can take time before the work of solving it begins.

points.explanation: The answer says to take criticism seriously and not dismiss feedback, including feedback previously explained away or discarded.
The answer recommends candid peer feedback and working on the resulting development area, but does not clearly include the specific advice to consider that a trusted peer may be right.
